patients.label: Case 1: 64-year-old female with septic shock and bilateral adrenal haemorrhage

identity_evidence.quote: A 64-year-old female (case demographics) was admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) with fulminant septic shock secondary to pneumonia. This was her third presentation to the emergency department within a span of several days with an unresolved chest infection with repeated courses of antibiotics. On presentation, she was profoundly hypotensive despite fluid resuscitation, hypothermic, and exhibited altered mental status (Table 1).

attribution_limitations: Admission narrative deranged clotting parameters conflicts with Table 2 normal clotting profile; neither treated as resolved.

patients.label: Case 2: 72-year-old man with COPD, pulmonary emboli and unilateral adrenal haemorrhage

identity_evidence.quote: A 72-year-old man with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), hypertension, osteoporosis, and prior subarachnoid haemorrhages presented after an unwitnessed fall. He reported left-sided chest pain from the evening before and was later found on the floor, having been unable to summon help. He had no memory of the event. He had a background of chronic hyponatremia and was being treated for an infective exacerbation of COPD with antibiotics and regular nebuliser. Initial blood test showed raised white cell count (WCC) and CRP (Table 3).

patients.label: Case 3: 42-year-old man with JAK2-positive essential thrombocythaemia and influenza-associated adenoma haemorrhage

identity_evidence.quote: A 42-year-old man came with acute diffuse abdominal pain after two days of flu-like symptoms (fever, malaise, and myalgia) on the background of essential thrombocythemia (JAK2-positive) and had been taking aspirin for that. He was diagnosed with essential thrombocythemia about three years ago, incidentally, when he was admitted to the hospital with COVID pneumonitis and was started on aspirin from the haematology team. In this admission, his onset of abdominal pain was abrupt and moderate in severity (scoring 6/10), associated with nausea, lethargy, decreased oral intake, and altered bowel movements without any urinary symptoms.

attribution_limitations: Abstract states steroid therapy administered in two cases, but p3 management explicitly no AH-specific treatment and no hormonal insufficiency; no p3 steroid administration inferred.

claims.text: Deterioration prompted empiric steroids for suspected adrenal insufficiency. CT followed by MRI showed bilateral AH, with low morning cortisol 44 nmol/L and primary adrenal crisis/Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome. IV hydrocortisone 100 mg then 50 mg QDS, IV antibiotics/fluid and ICU monitoring led to stabilisation; no vasopressor was needed. Oral hydrocortisone/fludrocortisone followed, but adrenal function remained impaired at five months, requiring ongoing replacement.

identity_evidence.quote: A 72-year-old man with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), hypertension, osteoporosis, and prior subarachnoid haemorrhages presented after an unwitnessed fall. He reported left-sided chest pain from the evening before and was later found on the floor, having been unable to summon help. He had no memory of the event. He had a background of chronic hyponatremia and was being treated for an infective exacerbation of COPD with antibiotics and regular nebuliser. Initial blood test showed raised white cell count (WCC) and CRP (Table 3).

claims.text: A 72-year-old man with severe COPD, hypertension, osteoporosis, previous subarachnoid haemorrhages and chronic hyponatremia presented after an unwitnessed fall with amnesia and preceding left chest pain. Suspected infective COPD exacerbation was treated with antibiotics/nebuliser. Admission inflammatory markers were high; ACS was excluded and bronchoscopic endobronchial lesions absent.

evidence.quote: A 72-year-old man with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), hypertension, osteoporosis, and prior subarachnoid haemorrhages presented after an unwitnessed fall. He reported left-sided chest pain from the evening before and was later found on the floor, having been unable to summon help. He had no memory of the event. He had a background of chronic hyponatremia and was being treated for an infective exacerbation of COPD with antibiotics and regular nebuliser. Initial blood test showed raised white cell count (WCC) and CRP (Table 3).

claims.text: Day 3 CTPA identified bilateral pulmonary emboli and a 34 mm probable left adrenal haemorrhage; MRI three days later measured 32 x 31 mm without interval change. Cortisol 579 nmol/L was described as normal, with no overt adrenal insufficiency/crisis; conservative AH management required no steroids/surgery. Tazocin, fluids, oxygen and apixaban were given. MRI about three months later showed 21 x 13 mm left lesion and normal right gland. Respiratory improvement followed by declining baseline function led to home NIV; endocrinology review and six-month MRI remained planned.

Endocrine testing included cortisol, ACTH, renin, and aldosterone levels; infectious screens included TB, malaria, and other opportunistic pathogens. Plasma metanephrines were normal. Aldosterone was 380 pmol/L (normal range 90-700), renin activity 5.2 nmol/L/hr (elevated relative to reference 0.5-3.5), giving an aldosterone/renin ratio of 73 (<80: not consistent with primary aldosteronism) (aldosterone blood test was taken in the lying position, and the patient was on his regular losartan for hypertension at that time).
Initial blood test showed raised CRP and neutrophils. He was found to be positive for influenza A on nasal swab PCR (Table 5).

A non-contrast CT was performed to r/o acute abdomen as a cause of persistent abdominal pain, which revealed a soft tissue lesion in the left upper quadrant between the pancreas, spleen, and kidney. To further characterise, a contrast CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis (CT TAP) was performed, which demonstrated an enhancing nodule/mass in the left adrenal region with adjacent ill-defined soft tissue, raising concern for adrenal pathology, including haemorrhage or infection as the likely cause of abdominal pain.

claims.text: A 42-year-old man with JAK2-positive essential thrombocythemia diagnosed incidentally during COVID pneumonitis admission about three years earlier, on aspirin and regular losartan for hypertension, developed abrupt moderate 6/10 diffuse abdominal pain after two days of flu-like symptoms. Nausea, lethargy, poor oral intake and altered bowel movements occurred without urinary symptoms. Influenza A nasal PCR was positive, with thrombocytosis, lymphopenia, high neutrophils/CRP and hypokalaemia; blood culture showed no growth.

claims.text: Non-contrast then contrast CT localised a left adrenal lesion with haemorrhage/infection differential. Endocrine screening showed normal plasma metanephrines, aldosterone 380 pmol/L and renin 5.2 nmol/L/hr with ratio 73 interpreted against primary aldosteronism; cortisol/ACTH and infectious screening results were not reported. IV antibiotics, oseltamivir, potassium replacement and supportive care were given; no AH-specific treatment was needed. Post-discharge MRI showed stable 2.7 x 2.5 cm lipid-rich haemorrhagic adenoma; later endocrine review was asymptomatic, six-month MRI stable without malignancy, and renal MRA showed no stenosis. Outpatient hormonal surveillance continued; imaging diagnosis lacked tissue verification.

events.description: Functional endocrine and infectious workup, normal plasma metanephrines and elevated renin

evidence.quote: A 42-year-old man came with acute diffuse abdominal pain after two days of flu-like symptoms (fever, malaise, and myalgia) on the background of essential thrombocythemia (JAK2-positive) and had been taking aspirin for that. He was diagnosed with essential thrombocythemia about three years ago, incidentally, when he was admitted to the hospital with COVID pneumonitis and was started on aspirin from the haematology team. In this admission, his onset of abdominal pain was abrupt and moderate in severity (scoring 6/10), associated with nausea, lethargy, decreased oral intake, and altered bowel movements without any urinary symptoms.

evidence.quote: During the endocrine clinic review, the patient was asymptomatic. A repeat MRI at six months later showed stability, no interval growth, and no evidence of malignancy. An MRA of renal arteries was scheduled due to elevated renin levels as per guidelines, which showed no stenosis, excluding secondary hyperaldosteronism. He was followed up in the outpatient endocrine clinic for hormonal surveillance.
